sections.heading_text: Where this book sits on the shelf
sections.topic_sentence: Two books frame what this one attempts.

sections.heading_text: The premise: mechanize discipline
sections.topic_sentence: The first is **Software Engineering at Google** (Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, 2020), whose premise this book shares: engineering discipline should be *mechanized, not remembered* — pushed into review, testing, tooling, and culture so that correctness does not depend on any one engineer keeping a rule in their head.

sections.heading_text: The grammar: patterns, and two theses
sections.topic_sentence: The second is the **Gang of Four's** *Design Patterns* (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, and Vlissides, 1994), whose lasting contribution was less any single pattern than the *form* — name, recurring problem, solution shape, consequences, known uses — written so an engineer could reach for a vetted answer instead of re-deriving one.

sections.heading_text: Three ways to run a fleet
sections.topic_sentence: The hard problem of building software with agents is simple to state: the tools are fast and the tools are unreliable.

sections.heading_text: The through-line, and who it is for
sections.topic_sentence: The through-line is a single idea; hold every chapter against it.

sections.heading_text: A map of the book
sections.topic_sentence: Five parts, and they compose in a particular order.

sections.heading_text: Acknowledgments
sections.topic_sentence: I thank K.

sections.heading_text: What this book is about (and what it is not)
sections.topic_sentence: Of course, not every programming task needs the machinery this book describes.

points.text: The first judgment is whether a task needs governed autonomy.

sections.heading_text: The two modes
sections.topic_sentence: Start at the decision on the left.

points.text: Mode forks on the work's size and difficulty.
One-shot scripting fits a small task needing no subtle reasoning.
Supervised autonomy supplies four things in two groups.
Each later part develops one of the four elements.

sections.heading_text: Where the emphasis falls
sections.topic_sentence: This book is about both modes.

points.text: Misjudging the mode either way is expensive.
Leash length follows training-data density and model capability.
The book's weight falls on supervised autonomy.
Code is cheap; turn the fabricator into a production line.

sections.heading_text: The printer
sections.topic_sentence: Think of a 3D printer.

points.text: The 3D printer is the book's governing metaphor.

sections.heading_text: An open-ended technology
sections.topic_sentence: A 3D printer belongs to a rare class of technology — the *open-ended* kind — alongside the invention of writing and the printing press.

points.text: An open-ended technology arrives with no list; people invent genres.
Generative AI is open-ended; this book takes one genre.
The quality floor was the price; agents make it cheap.

sections.heading_text: A picture is not enough
sections.topic_sentence: Everyone can sketch a piece of software.

points.text: Anyone can picture software, but a picture will not print.
A printer needs a structural model plus print notes.
Agents need the build instructions, not just the picture.

sections.heading_text: Whose fault is it?
sections.topic_sentence: Here is the shift in posture the whole book turns on.

points.text: An agent is a printer, not a stapler; suspect instructions.
Models build anything you can explain; explaining is the discipline.
Building anything you describe is both promise and danger.
Speed does not cause the danger; it exposes it.
The running example is a shipped system, not a toy.

sections.heading_text: Everything is a loop
sections.topic_sentence: An agent runs in a loop, and the loop has a fixed shape.

points.text: Agent work is a loop of fixed shape.
Engineering a loop starts with a measurable metric.
The orchestrator is a worked loop written as a model.

sections.heading_text: Give it a model of the world

points.text: Vibe coding sees an I/O device; engineering, a system.
The split is what counts as proof a change works.
The world-model is the input the agent reasons over.
A foundation model is a probabilistic reasoning machine.
Agent behavior is a search over a vast space.
Loop and model condition the agent's probability distribution.
A model aims the search and shrinks what is held.
The printer metaphor breaks at determinism versus probability.

preamble_points.text: Two ideas carry the book: the loop and the model.

sections.heading_text: The lifecycle it keeps
sections.topic_sentence: Engineering ran on the same handful of activities long before software, and software inherits them whole: **requirements** (find out what the system must do, and for whom — usually the hard part, since the people who need it cannot state it), **specification** (say what it will do, precisely enough to check later), **design** (decide the parts, the seams, and how the whole meets its constraints), **implementation** (build it — for software, write the code), **validation** (show the built thing meets the spec), and **maintenance** (change it over the long life without breaking what already works).

points.text: Every engineering discipline shares six activities.
Software loosens physics, copies free, stays malleable.
Process models reorder the activities, never replace them.

sections.heading_text: The two seats
sections.topic_sentence: Two words for two jobs, and this book keeps them apart.

points.text: The engineer authors intent; the developer writes code.
MAGE reassigns exactly one seat: the developer's.
The role shrinks nothing; judgment grows more consequential.
Engineers always had models; writing them down stopped paying.

sections.heading_text: SDLC to SELC
sections.topic_sentence: The field's own name for the lifecycle gives the old arrangement away: SDLC, the software *development* life cycle.

points.text: SDLC names the activity the human no longer performs.
Rename it SELC: the software engineering life cycle.
Delegating the keystrokes keeps accountability intact.

sections.heading_text: A different seat is a different discipline
sections.topic_sentence: Same lifecycle, then; no new phases.

points.text: Same phases; the reassigned seat remakes the discipline.
Executing from models repeats the assembly-to-code move.
The rest of the book equips the engineer's seat.

preamble_points.text: Software's engineer/developer split kept collapsing; agents hold it apart.

sections.heading_text: First, four definitions
sections.topic_sentence: Before the walk, I owe you four definitions: *engineering*, *software engineering*, *agent*, and *model*.

points.text: Four definitions carry the book's argument.
Articulated trade-offs separate the engineer from the technician.
Engineers predict outcomes before building.
Software engineering selects the artifact before building it.
Intelligence devises means to goals within constraints.
Controllable, not controlled, is why governance exists.
The models are the agent's knowledge base.
Perceive-and-act builds agents; controllability governs them.
Model fidelity trades against reasoning cost.
A blueprint model specifies; the build may not diverge.
A model is constraint, blueprint, and knowledge base.
The word model does double duty; context disambiguates.
The four definitions' relations summarize the whole book.

sections.heading_text: The four layers
sections.topic_sentence: **At the bottom sits the foundation model.** It comes from a commercial vendor or an open-weight release, and it is a general language reasoner, able to *induce* an understanding of your environment — though that induction is expensive, and it happens fresh every time.

points.text: Tell the model where to look; spare its reasoning.
The model reasons over a world representation, so equip it.
The harness manages the context window and holds two mechanisms.
Skills are soft, hooks are hard, tools take deterministic action.
Write down the engineering environment; it offers git hooks.
Static analysis makes a mistake class structurally impossible.

sections.heading_text: Every layer is a place to steer
sections.topic_sentence: Read the stack as a list of opportunities, because that is what it is.

points.text: Read each layer as an injection opportunity.
Every layer serves one goal: narrow the agent's search.
Mechanisms interact; the interplay is its own problem.
The stack grounds both the Modeling and Alignment theses.

preamble_points.text: The agent stack has four layers, each an injection point.

sections.heading_text: Words are soft, code is verbose, a model is the sweet spot
sections.topic_sentence: Your first governance mechanism is the prompt, because the agent is a language model and words are how you talk to it.

points.text: Words are soft; agents need precision that humans do not.
Code is precise but too verbose; a model is between.
A model is a cheap, honest approximation you reason over.

sections.heading_text: Why the models drifted — and why that changes now
sections.topic_sentence: The models are the map; the code is the territory.

points.text: Model is map, code is territory; hand-sync drifts.
A hand-maintained model rots the moment its maintainer stops.
Agents flip it: they reason over models, not the code.
The model shifts with the move; keep a linked set.
A drift gate makes "map equals territory" a checked property.

sections.heading_text: Why agents don't reach for models on their own — a conjecture
sections.topic_sentence: Here a skeptic has a fair question.

points.text: The agent's reluctance to model echoes its corpus, not merit.

sections.heading_text: The apex of the documentation hierarchy is a typed model
sections.topic_sentence: Step back from drift for a moment and look at what you actually hand an agent to work from.

points.text: You hand an agent a hierarchy of partial, drifting descriptions.
Nothing binds docs, code, and tests, so drift is default.
The hierarchy's apex is a typed model that binds everything.
The typed model is the one description that cannot lie.
Structured English stops one rung short; a checker cannot act.

sections.heading_text: A drift check proves agreement, not correctness
sections.topic_sentence: The claim I just made hides a trap, and the book's enthusiasm for drift gates can be misread into a dangerous half-truth.

points.text: A drift gate proves agreement, not correctness.
A mirror reflects code; only a spec catches wrong.
Deciding what belongs in the model is the essential residual.

sections.heading_text: Just execute the model? A short history of CASE and MDA
sections.topic_sentence: If the typed model is where you now start, an old idea says to finish there too: skip the code and *execute the model directly*.

points.text: Executing the model directly is a forty-year-old idea.
CASE and MDA were the named dreams of executable models.
Executable models failed on tempo; teams generate key parts.
How far to model is a spectrum: strength for changeability.
The sweet spot moved outward and is still moving.

sections.heading_text: The semantic gap
sections.topic_sentence: Enforce a property at the wrong level and it slips through; [ref:semantic-gap] shows the fix — lift the check to where the meaning is legible.

points.text: Enforce a property at the wrong level; it slips through.
Checking model drift at the commit is the wrong granularity.
The semantic gap is enforcing at the wrong level.
Enforce where the property is legible: at agent-return.

sections.heading_text: A worked example: the context-fullness bank-hook
sections.topic_sentence: Let me give you a second instance of the semantic gap, one that lives not in the product but in the operator's own loop.

points.text: Compaction is a lossy guess; the harness sits below meaning.

sections.heading_text: The fix: a hook one level up, checking two things
sections.topic_sentence: So I moved the check up to where the property *is* legible: the operator's loop.

points.text: The fix is a hook checking fullness and staleness together.

sections.heading_text: Why both conditions, and not one
sections.topic_sentence: Why insist on both conditions?

points.text: A single loose condition fires too often, driving the ouroboros.

sections.heading_text: The honest part: the pre-compact hook is the wrong hook
sections.topic_sentence: I want to be straight about a compromise buried in this, because it is the kind of thing the semantic-gap idea should make you notice rather than paper over.

points.text: The pre-compact hook fires too late; the bank trips compaction.
With no clean rung, a roughly-right hook beats both.

preamble_points.text: Inject a model, but check it at the right level.

sections.heading_text: Ex-ante: everything you can decide up front
sections.topic_sentence: Some things you genuinely know from the beginning, and you should write every one of them down.

points.text: Write down what you know; determinize it with cheap checks.

sections.heading_text: Ex-post: everything you learn by building
sections.topic_sentence: But you will not know everything, and pretending otherwise is the mistake.

points.text: You build governance ex-post, as failures reveal themselves.
Ex-post is where most real mechanisms come from.
Hold a quality goal with a mechanism that keeps it.

sections.heading_text: Constraints and sensors
sections.topic_sentence: A mechanism is one of two moves — prevent the mistake, or catch it — and [ref:constraint-vs-sensor] draws the split.

points.text: A mechanism is one of two moves: prevent, or catch.
Words are a probability flip; determinize them into a gate.
A sensor detects drift after the fact and costs iterations.
A sensor is only as good as its observability.
A constraint prevents drift within the iteration, costing none.
Form and move are two independent axes.
Most mechanisms are a package; tag the primary move.
A purely organizational answer is all sensors, removing no class.
Determinize what you can; convert every surprise into a mechanism.

sections.heading_text: The residual: goals no mechanism reaches
sections.topic_sentence: That closing line reads as if it settles everything.

points.text: Some goals split into neither, being an absence nobody specified.
The residual is a human job setting the throughput ceiling.
The residual is the complement of both moves, not soft.
Naming the residual is the honest edge that earns trust.
The residual is not fixed; authoring the spec shrinks it.

preamble_points.text: A governed environment has an ex-ante and ex-post half.

sections.heading_text: Lifecycles first, then the failure map
sections.topic_sentence: Start with the lifecycles, because everything else hangs off them.

points.text: A lifecycle: write the healthy path, then map failures.
FMEA: name each failure's way out and prohibition.
Pair each prohibition with its sanctioned way out.

sections.heading_text: Runbooks: split the deterministic from the judgment
sections.topic_sentence: Once the healthy path and the failure map are written, the thing you hand the agent is a **runbook** (or playbook): the steps to take, whether recovering from a failure or working a fresh ticket.

points.text: A runbook splits into deterministic and judgment steps.
Deterministic steps get executable tools, not improvisation.
Determinizing buys a trace with two consumers.

sections.heading_text: The judgment parts: the roughest algorithm that still fits
sections.topic_sentence: **The judgment parts get the roughest algorithm that still fits.** For a well-constrained decision, write the algorithm down and let the agent do the glue.

points.text: Judgment steps get the roughest algorithm that fits.
A judgment that is a measurement gets a rubric.
The pre-canned brief templates delegation itself.

preamble_points.text: The agent lacks your operating context; write it down.

sections.heading_text: Measure one level deeper
sections.topic_sentence: John Ousterhout gives the rule in one line: **measure one level deeper than the number you think you want.** A metric earns its place only when it drives a decision, and the surface number usually cannot; the deeper the measurement, the nearer it sits to the decision it must drive.

points.text: Measure one level deeper; the surface number cannot act.
A cloud bill reports; splitting it by service acts.
Boot time, one level deeper: fix the slow phase.
Line coverage is the invoice number; go deeper.
Metrics run hard to soft; don't confuse the two.

sections.heading_text: The hard end: cold-start latency, machine-read and model-fed
sections.topic_sentence: Start at the deterministic end, where a metric is a millisecond number nobody argues about.

points.text: Cold-start latency reads obviously as the scale-from-zero penalty.
The deeper number named runtime init, not scale-from-zero.
Spot-checking fails; a model sums the longest cold-start path.
The hard end's defining move: the number feeds the model.
Automate map upkeep into the machine, not a reminder.
As-built: the seam is in, the data catches up.

sections.heading_text: The flagship: coverage measured one level deeper
sections.topic_sentence: Now the middle of the spectrum, and the chapter's teaching example: the "measure one level deeper" rule applied to the number that most often gets it wrong.

points.text: Line coverage answers a syntactic question, not the semantic one.
The fix joins a traceability graph to the coverage oracle.
The composition counts model claims and reports a named verdict.
The genre check names this requirements-based coverage.
One primitive supports several aggregations, each a different decision.
The honesty layer reports a breakdown, not a percentage.
Measuring one level deeper cost a join, not a rebuild.

sections.heading_text: The soft end: doc-derived tests
sections.topic_sentence: Slide to the far end of the spectrum, where the metric stops being a number a threshold can act on and becomes a judgment a human has to make.

points.text: A doc-derived test pins a doc-claim; its metric is soft.
Gating this soft signal manufactures hollow tests.

sections.heading_text: The model runs the machinery
sections.topic_sentence: The hard end and the flagship follow the same pattern.

points.text: The model is machinery, not a picture of it.
A component-distance grade drives a gate three ways.
The grade is a model-read metric driving a sensor.

sections.heading_text: A compact reference
sections.topic_sentence: [ref:metrics-table] collects every metric — the decision each drives, where it sits on the hard-soft axis, and who reads it.

points.text: Every row names a decision, or was measured too shallow.

preamble_points.text: A metric is the sensing half of the agent loop.
The metric comes first; it must drive a decision.

sections.heading_text: Drawing what lies between the controls
sections.topic_sentence: The Governance Graph draws it.

points.text: Nodes are mechanisms; edges are conflicts over a shared resource.
The shared resource is the only cross-lifecycle coupling surface.
The graph is the catalogue's dynamic dual.
The graph makes "mechanisms compose" explicit and checkable.

sections.heading_text: When the hooks aren't yours
sections.topic_sentence: Every mechanism so far was one you wrote.

points.text: Outside hooks extend the graph without changing its shape.
An unanalyzed outside hook conflicts with everything on its slot.
Composing outside governance is checking the merged graph for contradiction.

sections.heading_text: Keeping the model honest
sections.topic_sentence: Two disciplines keep the model honest, and both are the book's.

points.text: Keep the graph symbol-anchored and descriptive, not aspirational.

preamble_points.text: A control system has a failure a list cannot show.
A collision lives between two controls, drawn nowhere.

sections.heading_text: The expense that buried MBSE is the one a fleet pays for free
sections.topic_sentence: Model-based systems engineering never failed on its ideas.

points.text: MBSE failed on upkeep, not on its ideas.
A fleet supplies MBSE's one fatal expense for nearly nothing.
One model is never the whole picture.
MBSE here means derived software models of discrete systems.
The model level buys fewer tokens, velocity, and quality together.

sections.heading_text: Data from the case study
sections.topic_sentence: The fewer-tokens leg is the one we can measure directly.

points.text: An A/B navigation pilot measured the fewer-tokens leg directly.
The pilot saved about 35% of tokens, zero accuracy lost.

sections.heading_text: Kruchten's 4+1, promoted from a closing sentence to the spine
sections.topic_sentence: The last chapter invoked Kruchten's **4+1 views** in a final sentence — "the reason one model is never enough." This Part promotes that sentence to its organizing structure.

points.text: This Part promotes Kruchten's 4+1 to its organizing spine.

sections.heading_text: What this book adds to 4+1: the drift gate
sections.topic_sentence: Kruchten, of course, described the views; he did not have a drift gate.

points.text: The book adds to 4+1 a drift gate per view.

sections.heading_text: The framework is a choice; the core is not
sections.topic_sentence: Making the model executable is why this Part is not really *about* 4+1.

points.text: An executable core makes a framework a projection.
Rival frameworks are renderings of one executable core.
A lens hides content but cannot invent it.
Hit the executable core; framework wars become projection choices.

sections.heading_text: The trunk: machinery that holds any view true
sections.topic_sentence: Before the views, one chapter of framing.

points.text: Shared trunk machinery makes every view executable and drift-proof.

sections.heading_text: Beat 1 — a model is derived and joined, never repeated
sections.topic_sentence: The last chapter warned against repetition: two models that say the same thing must now be kept in sync.

points.text: A model is derived and joined, never repeated.
Derivation and join are the cure for repetition.

sections.heading_text: Beat 2 — name the direction of derivation
sections.topic_sentence: A model and the code it concerns stay equal by derivation, and derivation runs in one of two directions.

points.text: Name the direction of derivation up front.
Most of the zoo is model-from-code; the codebase came first.

sections.heading_text: Beat 3 — every model traces to the code
sections.topic_sentence: A model earns trust only if you can get from a model element back to the lines that realize it, and forward from a line to the model element that governs it.

points.text: Every model traces to the code in both directions.
The template folds a traceability note into every page.
A zoo of drifted views is worse than none.
The round-trip must be derived, not snapshotted.
A resolving edge is both drift-detection and navigation.

sections.heading_text: Keeping the models honest — the traceability substrate
sections.topic_sentence: DocAble did not design this up front.

points.text: The substrate was built from what broke, not designed.
A stale model makes agents plan against a dead system.
A hand-maintained checklist rots the moment the code moves.

sections.heading_text: Reading the fix off real drift
sections.topic_sentence: The right sensor was read off real drift rather than guessed.

points.text: The fix was read off real drift, not guessed.
The graph joins existing nodes by re-proved edges.

sections.heading_text: Two decisions that make the graph resist rot

points.text: The symbol walk fires slowly because cadence follows cost.
Derived sensors defend; snapshotted ones drift.

sections.heading_text: How to read a model page
sections.topic_sentence: Every model in this Part is rendered by filling the same five-field template.

points.text: Every model page fills the same five-field template.
The five fields answer the reader's five questions.

sections.heading_text: The service-flow / API model
sections.topic_sentence: *The typed source-of-truth for a service-oriented architecture — its services, their endpoints, their authentication, and the wiring between them — from which the access policy and environment wiring are generated and against which the real call graph is checked.*

points.text: The service-flow model is a service architecture's typed source-of-truth.
The model answers three questions scattered config cannot.
The service-flow model derives in both directions.

sections.heading_text: The domain registries
sections.topic_sentence: The domain registries are the frozen tables the service-flow model rests on: the file types the system handles, its known conformance gaps, its scheduled jobs, its user-facing surfaces.

points.text: Frozen registries are the single source every consumer joins.

preamble_points.text: The Logical view answers what the system is.
Two general types and two real models carry the view.
A data-flow diagram traces data across transforms.
An inheritance hierarchy shows which specializations exist.

sections.heading_text: Formal invariant verification
sections.topic_sentence: Formal invariant verification is the backbone the other three models hang their invariant tables on.

points.text: An invariant's temporal form routes its exhaustive checker.

sections.heading_text: The synchronization model
sections.topic_sentence: *A typed registry that models the system's synchronization behavior — every OS-level lock, which shared resource it guards, and the required acquisition ordering — so concurrency contracts are declared and checkable, not tribal.*

points.text: The sync model declares every lock and its ordering.
It assesses lock coverage and deadlock-freedom.
The sync model derives from code by lock path.

sections.heading_text: Two ways to make a concurrent write safe: the mediator and the single-writer registries
sections.topic_sentence: The synchronization model catalogs the raw locks.

points.text: Capping how-many and allowing exactly-one fail differently.

sections.heading_text: The mediator registry
sections.topic_sentence: The mediator registry is the *how-many* half.

points.text: The mediator registry caps how many run at once.

sections.heading_text: The single-writer registry
sections.topic_sentence: The single-writer registry is the *exactly-one* half, and its failure mode is what makes it a separate model.

points.text: The single-writer registry allows exactly one writer.

preamble_points.text: The Process view asks what runs at once.
Here invariants become predicates over an order of events.
An automaton is states and their legal transitions.
Claims about order over time need temporal logic.
An invariant's temporal shape derives its checker.
Model checking explores exhaustively where a test samples.

sections.heading_text: The component & zone model
sections.topic_sentence: *A typed catalog of every component's code zone — its focus directories, its tags, its boundary kind, its external seams, its read surfaces — so "which component owns this file, and what may touch it" is a queried fact rather than a per-tool guess.*

points.text: The component-zone model makes ownership a queried fact.
It assesses ownership correctness and boundary soundness.
The component-zone model derives from the directory tree.

sections.heading_text: The rule-metadata registry
sections.topic_sentence: The rule-metadata registry is the self-referential slice of the domain registries: the governance rules' own metadata, and so the model the governance machinery — and this book — are partly governed by.

points.text: Rule metadata lives beside each rule and generates the index.

preamble_points.text: The Development view maps how the source is organized.
One general type and two real models carry the view.
A bill of materials demands a complete dependency manifest.

sections.heading_text: The performance/cost view: mostly embodied, one honest gap
sections.topic_sentence: The zoo names a performance and cost model as a general type, and the framework supports it.

points.text: The cost view is partly embodied; the book says so.
A per-host profile rations load and cost.
Model only where a failure lives; latency slice stayed empty.
Scale-to-zero shipped without a latency model; production paid.

sections.heading_text: The deployment & tier topology model
sections.topic_sentence: *The typed statement of where things run — each service's name, its layer, and its tier — from which the deploy scripts and layering lints reason about a declared topology rather than scattered constants, and against which the real deploy table is reconciled.*

points.text: The topology model declares where each service deploys.
It assesses deployment parity and layer-boundary soundness.
The parity check runs both directions or misses drift.
The topology model derives from the deploy table.

sections.heading_text: The invariant-DAG execution policy
sections.topic_sentence: *A deploy graph whose edges carry a typed intent — correctness, cost-gate, or load — kept host-identical, plus a typed Scheduler that reads a per-host profile and rations load and cost so one host fans work out while a scarce one serializes it.*

points.text: A host-identical graph plus a Scheduler rations per host.
It assesses graph portability and rationing correctness.
The execution plan derives from the host profile.

sections.heading_text: The control↔substrate dependency model
sections.topic_sentence: The substrate-dependency model makes each governance mechanism declare, as typed metadata, the substrate assumption it bakes in — bound to one substrate, substrate-aware, or substrate-agnostic.

points.text: Declared substrate stances make a migration blast radius computable.

preamble_points.text: The Physical view maps where the parts run.
A performance-cost model anchors the view, one honest gap.

sections.heading_text: The user-journey model
sections.topic_sentence: The user-journey model makes the product's journeys first-class typed entities — each an actor pursuing a goal through ordered steps, every boundary-crossing step joined to the endpoint it calls.

points.text: The user-journey model copies nothing; the zoo joins to it.

sections.heading_text: The agent-orchestration model
sections.topic_sentence: The agent-orchestration model is the developer-journey counterpart — the scenarios view pointed at the fleet rather than the user.

points.text: Method parity governs the fleet like the product it ships.

sections.heading_text: Journey-criticality → test-placement
sections.topic_sentence: This model — the **Selector** in the join below — derives which environment tier a journey's tests run in from the journey's criticality: a `MAJOR` part runs the fast local tier and the full staging matrix, a `MINOR` part runs staging only.

points.text: A journey's criticality derives its test tier, never stored.

sections.heading_text: Coverage → model-node mapping
sections.topic_sentence: Coverage-to-node mapping projects the test suite's coverage onto the model's *nodes* — states, seams, invariants, journey endpoints — instead of its lines.

points.text: Projecting coverage onto nodes makes an untested invariant visible.

A flow-only closure on a major journey is a finding.

sections.heading_text: Lessons Learned

points.text: The takeaway was a methodology, not a model.

points.text: Three ways to run an agent; pick by risk.
